versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 By now Abraham was old and well along in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way. 2 So Abraham instructed the chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned, “Place your hand under my thigh, 3 and I will have you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling, 4 but will go to my country and my kindred to take a wife for my son Isaac.”
5 The servant asked him, “What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this land? Shall I then take your son back to the land from which you came?”

6 Abraham replied, “Make sure that you do not take my son back there. 7 The LORD, the God of heaven, who brought me from my father’s house and my native land, who spoke to me and promised me on oath, saying, ‘To your offspring I will give this land’—He will send His angel before you so that you can take a wife for my son from there. 8 And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine. Only do not take my son back there.”
9 So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and swore an oath to him concerning this matter.

10 Then the servant took ten of his master’s camels and departed with all manner of good things from his master in hand. And he set out for Nahor’s hometown in Aram-naharaim. 11 As evening approached, he made the camels kneel down near the well outside the town at the time when the women went out to draw water.

12 “O LORD, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham. 13 Here I am, standing beside the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water. 14 Now may it happen that the girl to whom I say, ‘Please let down your jar that I may drink,’ and who responds, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well’—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I will know that You have shown kindness to my master.”

context_lines: Abraham, now old, sends the chief servant of his household to seek a wife for Isaac among his relatives. The servant is trusted with Abraham's possessions, but this chapter does not name him. Abraham binds him by an oath, expressed by placing a hand under his thigh. The account records the gesture without explaining all of its cultural meaning.

Two instructions govern the mission: the wife must come from Abraham's kindred rather than the Canaanites, and Isaac must not be taken back to the country Abraham left. Abraham links his confidence to God's promise of this land to his offspring. If the woman is unwilling to come, the servant is released from the oath; he is not authorized to force the outcome.

The servant travels with ten camels to Nahor's town in Aram-naharaim and stops beside the well as women come to draw water. He asks God to show kindness to Abraham by identifying the appointed woman through her offering water to him and his camels. That response would show generous service as well as answer his particular request.

The word translated kindness is חֶסֶד, *ḥesed* (KHEH-sed). [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/2617.htm) gives kindness and lovingkindness among its meanings and cites this chapter. The servant is asking for God's faithful care toward Abraham to take practical shape in this journey.
common_interpretation_lines: A common Christian reading sees prayer for guidance joined with a task carried out under Abraham's instructions. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 24:12–15](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) welcome specific prayer and attention to God's care, while warning against prescribing to God exactly how He must act. The account describes this servant's request; it does not promise that every reader can identify a spouse by arranging the same sort of test.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The search serves a purpose larger than finding a suitable household match: the promised family through Isaac must continue. Abraham refuses to secure that future by undoing God's call to the land. His confidence grows from the promise already given, and the servant seeks help while working within that direction.

This also illustrates a theme carried into [James 1:5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/james/1.htm): people who lack wisdom can ask God for it. James encourages that dependence without giving a method of creating signs. The connection is the shared call to seek God's help with a real responsibility, rather than to treat the events at the well as a guaranteed formula for every decision.
